claim: Apical actin caps in the early syncytial Drosophila embryo undergo cyclic behaviors of formation and disassembly on relatively short time scales.
source: The apical actin caps in the early syncytial Drosophila embryo are highly active structures that undergo cyclic behaviors of formation and disassembly on relatively short time scales.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the manuscript describing the dynamic nature of apical actin caps.

claim: mCh:MoeABD labeling method has been used extensively in the Drosophila embryo and well-represents endogenous filamentous actin dynamics.
source: This method of labeling has been used extensively in the Drosophila embryo and well-represents endogenous filamentous actin dynamics while avoiding problems that occur when fluorescent proteins are directly attached to actin or other labeling paradigms (such as Lifeact; Kiehart et al., 2000; Blankenship et al., 2006; Spracklen et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work and reference to supplementary figure data.

claim: Actin cap formation was imaged through four cycles that occur in the syncytial blastoderm (nuclear cycles 10–13).
source: Actin cap formation was imaged through the four cycles that occur in the syncytial blastoderm (nuclear cycles 10–13), and actin growth behaviors were analyzed (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–G; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing the imaging data.

claim: During the expansion phase, cycle 11 actin caps rapidly expand from small proto-caps to caps 15–18 µm in diameter and 206 µm2 in area on average within 2 min.
source: During the expansion phase, cycle 11 actin caps rapidly expand from small proto-caps to caps 15–18 µm in diameter and 206 µm2 in area on average within 2 min (Figure 1A–F).
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative measurements supported by figure references.

claim: Apical cap size increases almost sixfold during the expansion phase.
source: Apical cap size increases almost sixfold during this period and growth rates peak early during expansion (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: The claim is directly stated with quantitative data and supported by figure references.

claim: Despite exponential growth in cap size, actin intensity increases only mildly with a ~39% increase by the end of stabilization.
source: Interestingly, despite the exponential growth in cap size, the actin intensity increases only mildly, with a ~39% increase by the end of stabilization (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative measurements and is supported by figure reference.

claim: Actin recruitment is carefully regulated spatially such that the cap grows rapidly in total area but regional intensities do not increase proportionally.
source: This suggests that actin recruitment is carefully regulated spatially such that the cap grows rapidly in total area but regional intensities do not.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data regarding cap growth and intensity.

claim: The stabilization phase lasts for ~60 s with caps largely maintaining their size.
source: The following stabilization phase lasts for ~60 s with caps largely maintaining their size.
evidence: The claim provides a specific time measurement for a phase of cap dynamics.

claim: Cap heterogeneity drops by approximately one quarter of the maximum at the end of stabilization phase.
source: However, cap intensities begin to decrease and heterogeneity within the cap drops by approximately one quarter of the maximum at the end of stabilization phase (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: The claim provides quantitative measurement supported by figure references.

claim: The morphology of the cap during elongation switches from round to an elongated doughnut-like structure.
source: Interestingly, the morphology of the cap during elongation switches from round to an elongated doughnut-like structure and caps begin to lose intensity in internal actin populations (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim describes morphological changes observed in the data and supported by figure reference.

claim: Diaphanous and the Arp2/3 complex have been previously implicated in regulating actin nucleation at syncytial stages.
source: The Formin Diaphanous and the Arp2/3 complex have been previously implicated in regulating actin nucleation at these syncytial stages (Stevenson et al., 2002; Zallen et al., 2002; Grosshans et al., 2005; Cao et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Diaphanous appears to be the major regulator of furrow-associated F-actin according to published studies.
source: According to published studies, Diaphanous appears to be the major regulator of furrow-associated F-actin, while Arp2/3 has been implicated in apical actin formation (Grosshans et al., 2005; Cao et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018), although comprehensive time-lapse-based quantitation has been lacking.
evidence: The claim is based on published studies cited in the text.

claim: Arp2/3 has been implicated in apical actin formation according to published studies.
source: According to published studies, Diaphanous appears to be the major regulator of furrow-associated F-actin, while Arp2/3 has been implicated in apical actin formation (Grosshans et al., 2005; Cao et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2018), although comprehensive time-lapse-based quantitation has been lacking.
evidence: The claim is based on published studies cited in the text.

claim: Disruption of Diaphanous function deeply affects furrow-associated actin.
source: Consistent with previous results, disruption of Diaphanous function deeply affects furrow-associated actin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure reference showing experimental data.

claim: Diaphanous shows a significant contribution to the early expansion of actin caps.
source: However, Diaphanous also shows a significant contribution to the early expansion of actin caps.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental findings.

claim: Dia disrupted embryos have a ~35% reduction in cap area expansion.
source: Dia disrupted embryos have a ~ 35% reduction in cap area expansion, but a relatively mild 18% reduction in actin intensities and cap expansion rate (Figure 2A–H, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative measurements supported by figure references.

claim: Dia disrupted embryos have a relatively mild 18% reduction in actin intensities and cap expansion rate.
source: Dia disrupted embryos have a ~ 35% reduction in cap area expansion, but a relatively mild 18% reduction in actin intensities and cap expansion rate (Figure 2A–H, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative measurements supported by figure references.

claim: When Arp2/3 function is compromised there is an almost complete absence of cap expansion.
source: By contrast to Diaphanous, when Arp2/3 function is compromised there is an almost complete absence of cap expansion and cap actin intensities are reduced to 47% of wild-type levels (Figure 2A–H).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: When Arp2/3 function is compromised, cap actin intensities are reduced to 47% of wild-type levels.
source: By contrast to Diaphanous, when Arp2/3 function is compromised there is an almost complete absence of cap expansion and cap actin intensities are reduced to 47% of wild-type levels (Figure 2A–H).
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative measurements supported by figure references.

claim: The remaining actin structure in Arp2/3 compromised embryos appear to be hollowed out and missing internal actin populations.
source: Interestingly, the remaining actin structure appear to be hollowed out and missing internal actin populations (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim describes morphological observations supported by figure references.

claim: Disruption of Diaphanous function did not significantly affect Arp2/3 intensities as judged by ArpC1:GFP.
source: Although defective cap structures characteristic of the above described results were observed, disruption of Diaphanous function did not significantly affect Arp2/3 intensities (as judged by ArpC1:GFP), nor did Arp2/3 disruption affect anti-Diaphanous intensities in the remaining cap structures (anti-Diaphanous immunostaining; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: Arp2/3 disruption did not affect anti-Diaphanous intensities in the remaining cap structures.
source: Although defective cap structures characteristic of the above described results were observed, disruption of Diaphanous function did not significantly affect Arp2/3 intensities (as judged by ArpC1:GFP), nor did Arp2/3 disruption affect anti-Diaphanous intensities in the remaining cap structures (anti-Diaphanous immunostaining; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: Diaphanous and Arp2/3 both contribute to structuring apical actin caps.
source: These results show that Diaphanous and Arp2/3 both contribute to structuring apical actin caps, but that Arp2/3 is the major regulator of actin intensities and cap growth.
evidence: This is a summary statement of experimental findings.

claim: Arp2/3 is the major regulator of actin intensities and cap growth.
source: These results show that Diaphanous and Arp2/3 both contribute to structuring apical actin caps, but that Arp2/3 is the major regulator of actin intensities and cap growth.
evidence: This is a summary statement of experimental findings.

claim: The hollowed out internal cap structures and failure in cap expansion suggests a possible model in which Arp2/3 polymerizes F-actin internally.
source: The hollowed out internal cap structures as well as the failure in cap expansion also suggests a possible model in which Arp2/3 polymerizes F-actin internally, and the cap possesses a dispersion mechanism that flows F-actin filaments towards the edges so as to maintain consistent internal F-actin intensities.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the observed data.

claim: The cap possesses a dispersion mechanism that flows F-actin filaments towards the edges to maintain consistent internal F-actin intensities.
source: The hollowed out internal cap structures as well as the failure in cap expansion also suggests a possible model in which Arp2/3 polymerizes F-actin internally, and the cap possesses a dispersion mechanism that flows F-actin filaments towards the edges so as to maintain consistent internal F-actin intensities.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the observed data.

claim: Cortactin, DPod1, Coronin, and Scar have distinct functions in building F-actin caps.
source: Interestingly, these results identify distinct functions for Cortactin, DPod1, Coronin, and Scar in building F-actin caps (Figure 3D–K), while disrupting Carmil, Wasp, and Wash had little effect on caps (Figure 3L,M, Figure 3—figure supplement 1J–M).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: Disrupting Carmil, Wasp, and Wash had little effect on caps.
source: Interestingly, these results identify distinct functions for Cortactin, DPod1, Coronin, and Scar in building F-actin caps (Figure 3D–K), while disrupting Carmil, Wasp, and Wash had little effect on caps (Figure 3L,M, Figure 3—figure supplement 1J–M).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: Compromising Coronin function causes an immediate defect in the expansion phase of cap formation.
source: Compromising Coronin function causes an immediate defect in the expansion phase of cap formation (Figure 3G,G'), with actin intensities at ~70% of control levels (Figure 3C,F,G'').
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: Coronin disruption results in actin intensities at ~70% of control levels.
source: Compromising Coronin function causes an immediate defect in the expansion phase of cap formation (Figure 3G,G'), with actin intensities at ~70% of control levels (Figure 3C,F,G'').
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative measurements supported by figure references.

claim: Disrupting DPod1 function produces caps that expand at near wild-type levels and possess wild-type areas until they fail to maintain area size in the later stages of apical cap function.
source: By contrast, disrupting DPod1 function produces caps that expand at near wild-type levels and possess wild-type areas until they fail to maintain area size in the later stages of apical cap function (Figure 3E,E').
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: DPod1 disrupted embryos have dramatically reduced actin intensities throughout the cap area.
source: However, these embryos have dramatically reduced actin intensities throughout the cap area (Figure 3E'').
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure reference showing experimental data.

claim: In embryos with compromised Cortactin function, there is a normal burst of actin expansion, but after ~120 s actin caps do not continue to grow and steadily diminish in size.
source: In embryos with compromised Cortactin function, there is a normal burst of actin expansion, but after ~120 s actin caps do not continue to grow and steadily diminish in size, suggesting a role for Cortactin in growth at the cap periphery (Figure 3H,I–I'').
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: Cortactin has a role in growth at the cap periphery.
source: In embryos with compromised Cortactin function, there is a normal burst of actin expansion, but after ~120 s actin caps do not continue to grow and steadily diminish in size, suggesting a role for Cortactin in growth at the cap periphery (Figure 3H,I–I'').
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: F-actin intensities within the smaller cap in Cortactin disrupted embryos are at higher levels than control embryos.
source: Interestingly, F-actin intensities within the smaller cap are at higher levels than control embryos (Figure 3I'').
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure reference showing experimental data.

claim: Disrupting Scar function produces actin caps that show an early depletion of F-actin intensities followed by a delayed expansion phase in which the caps cannot fully reach control cap areas.
source: Disrupting Scar function produces actin caps that show an early depletion of F-actin intensities followed by a delayed expansion phase in which the caps cannot fully reach control cap areas (Figure 3J,K–K'').
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: The specificity and reproducibility of ANRP disruption phenotypes was confirmed with second, independent shRNA lines.
source: The specificity and reproducibility of these phenotype was confirmed with second, independent shRNA lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure reference showing experimental validation.

claim: Disrupting the Formin Diaphanous had no effect on Arp3:GFP localization at apical structures.
source: Disrupting the Formin Diaphanous had no effect on Arp3:GFP localization at apical structures (Figure 3N,O).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: Disruption of ArpC4 almost completely abolishes apical Arp3:GFP localization and intensity.
source: By contrast, disruption of ArpC4, one of the Arp2/3 complex subunits, almost completely abolishes apical Arp3:GFP localization and intensity (Figure 3N,O).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: DPod1 had the largest effect on Arp3:GFP localization among the tested ANRPs.
source: Interestingly, DPod1, which had the deepest impact on overall F-actin intensities, also had the largest effect on Arp3:GFP localization, while Coronin, Scar, and Cortactin showed intermediate Arp3:GFP recruitment defects.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Coronin, Scar, and Cortactin showed intermediate Arp3:GFP recruitment defects.
source: Interestingly, DPod1, which had the deepest impact on overall F-actin intensities, also had the largest effect on Arp3:GFP localization, while Coronin, Scar, and Cortactin showed intermediate Arp3:GFP recruitment defects.
evidence: The claim is directly stated as a summary of experimental findings.

claim: DPod1 is required for overall actin intensities.
source: Together, these results reveal distinct functions for individual ANRPs, with DPod1 being required for overall actin intensities, while Cortactin and Scar are necessary for cap expansion and maintenance.
evidence: This is a summary statement of experimental findings.

claim: Cortactin and Scar are necessary for cap expansion and maintenance.
source: Together, these results reveal distinct functions for individual ANRPs, with DPod1 being required for overall actin intensities, while Cortactin and Scar are necessary for cap expansion and maintenance.
evidence: This is a summary statement of experimental findings.

claim: Coronin has an early function, possibly in the cap center.
source: These results are also consistent with Coronin having an early function, possibly in the cap center, and Cortactin/Scar possessing a later function in controlling cap growth and maintenance of cap areas at the periphery.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Cortactin/Scar possess a later function in controlling cap growth and maintenance of cap areas at the periphery.
source: These results are also consistent with Coronin having an early function, possibly in the cap center, and Cortactin/Scar possessing a later function in controlling cap growth and maintenance of cap areas at the periphery.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Coronin and Scar have both intensity (at early phases) and cap size functions.
source: Coronin and Scar have both intensity (at early phases) and cap size functions, and Carmil, Wasp, and Wash have either minor or no contributions to cap dynamics.
evidence: This is a summary statement of experimental findings.

claim: Carmil, Wasp, and Wash have either minor or no contributions to cap dynamics.
source: Coronin and Scar have both intensity (at early phases) and cap size functions, and Carmil, Wasp, and Wash have either minor or no contributions to cap dynamics.
evidence: This is a summary statement of experimental findings.

claim: Coronin, Cortactin, and DPod1 are highly expressed during syncytial stages according to qPCR.
source: These results show that Coronin, Cortactin, and DPod1 are highly expressed and Carmil and Wash are present at low levels during syncytial stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure reference showing qPCR data.

claim: Carmil and Wash are present at low levels during syncytial stages according to qPCR.
source: These results show that Coronin, Cortactin, and DPod1 are highly expressed and Carmil and Wash are present at low levels during syncytial stages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure reference showing qPCR data.

claim: Dia, Wasp, and Scar have intermediate expression during syncytial stages.
source: Dia, Wasp, and Scar have intermediate expression.
evidence: This is a direct statement of qPCR results.

claim: A CRISPR-generated GFP knock-in at the endogenous Arp3 locus shows a strong localization to the apical cap with little localization to furrows.
source: A CRISPR-generated GFP knock-in at the endogenous Arp3 locus shows a strong localization to the apical cap with little localization to furrows, consistent with our functional data (Figure 3N, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing localization data.

claim: Neither UAS-driven Carmil nor Wasp localized to apical actin caps.
source: Neither UAS-driven Carmil nor Wasp localized to apical actin caps (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), again consistent with the above functional analysis indicating their disruption had little impact on apical cap dynamics.
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing localization data.

claim: UAS-driven Coronin, Cortactin, Scar, and DPod1 all displayed varying degrees of localization to actin caps.
source: UAS-driven Coronin, Cortactin, Scar, and DPod1 all displayed varying degrees of localization to actin caps (Figure 4A–D, Figure 4—source data 1), with endogenous CRISPR constructs or antibody stains showing similar patterns (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing localization data.

claim: Coronin and Cortactin possess a complementary localization in mature caps, with Cortactin enrichment occurring at the cap periphery, while Coronin possesses an enrichment in the cap interior.
source: One intriguing facet of these regulators' localization, however, is that Coronin and Cortactin possessed a complementary localization in mature caps, with Cortactin enrichment occurring at the cap periphery, while Coronin possesses an enrichment in the cap interior (temporal overlays in Figure 4F–I).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing localization data.

claim: The complementary localization of Coronin and Cortactin suggests a possible antagonism between them.
source: The complementary localization also suggests a possible antagonism between Coronin and Cortactin.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the localization data.

claim: In the absence of Coronin function, Cortactin fails to transition to the cap periphery.
source: Remarkably, this revealed that, in the absence of Coronin function, Cortactin fails to transition to the cap periphery, indicating that Coronin contributes to the ability of Cortactin to localize to the cell periphery to direct actin growth and the maintenance of cap edges (Figure 4J,K).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: Coronin contributes to the ability of Cortactin to localize to the cell periphery to direct actin growth and the maintenance of cap edges.
source: Remarkably, this revealed that, in the absence of Coronin function, Cortactin fails to transition to the cap periphery, indicating that Coronin contributes to the ability of Cortactin to localize to the cell periphery to direct actin growth and the maintenance of cap edges (Figure 4J,K).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Actin is highly dynamic in cortical cap populations with a half-time of recovery (T50) of only 8.2 s and a low immobile fraction of 17%.
source: These results revealed that actin is highly dynamic, with a half-time of recovery (T50) of only 8.2 s in the cap and a low immobile fraction of 17% (Figure 5A–D, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative measurements from FRAP experiments supported by figure references.

claim: Furrow-associated actin is more stable with a T50 of 15.1 s.
source: Furrow-associated actin is more stable with a T50 of 15.1 s (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative measurements from FRAP experiments supported by figure reference.

claim: Recovery rates are nearly identical when actin is directly labeled with GFP, demonstrating that tracking actin cap behaviors with the MoeABD:GFP accurately reflects actin dynamics.
source: These recovery rates are nearly identical when actin is directly labeled with GFP, again demonstrating that tracking actin cap behaviors with the MoeABD:GFP accurately reflects actin dynamics and that any on–off actin-binding rates by MoeABD:GFP are significantly slower than actin turnover rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing comparative FRAP data.

claim: Actin recovery is much faster when either Arp2/3 or Diaphanous function is disrupted.
source: Surprisingly, we found that actin recovery is much faster when either Arp2/3 or Diaphanous function is disrupted.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental findings from FRAP experiments.

claim: The half-time to recovery of actin intensities is nearly twice as fast in ArpC4 and Diaphanous shRNA embryos (4.2 s and 4.1 s respectively) compared to wild-type embryos.
source: Indeed, although actin intensities are much reduced, the half-time to recovery of these intensities is nearly twice as fast as in wild-type embryo (4.2 s and 4.1 s in ArpC4 and Diaphanous shRNA embryos, respectively; Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim provides specific quantitative measurements from FRAP experiments supported by figure reference.

claim: Injecting embryos with low levels of jasplakinolide to stabilize F-actin increased recovery times.
source: We therefore injected embryos with low levels of jasplakinolide to stabilize F-actin – under these conditions, recovery times increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: Reducing the G-actin availability by low-dose Latrunculin B injection slowed recovery times.
source: Similarly, reducing the G-actin availability by low-dose Latrunculin B injection also slowed recovery times (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: The enhanced FRAP recovery times are driven by increased rates of nucleation and polymerization due to higher free G-actin pools.
source: Given that both Diaphanous and Arp2/3 complex function are deeply implicated in directing actin growth and nucleation, and the fact that they are chronically depleted in these experiments, we would suggest that these results support the first model and argues that these complexes are in a strong competition for a limited pool of available G-actin monomers.
evidence: This is an interpretation and proposed model to explain the FRAP data.

claim: Diaphanous and Arp2/3 complexes are in a strong competition for a limited pool of available G-actin monomers.
source: Given that both Diaphanous and Arp2/3 complex function are deeply implicated in directing actin growth and nucleation, and the fact that they are chronically depleted in these experiments, we would suggest that these results support the first model and argues that these complexes are in a strong competition for a limited pool of available G-actin monomers.
evidence: This is an interpretation and proposed model to explain the FRAP data.

claim: FRAP analysis after disrupting Cofilin function did not significantly slow down FRAP recovery times.
source: Consistent with this, FRAP analysis after disrupting Cofilin function (known as twinstar in Drosophila) did not significantly slow down FRAP recovery times (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: Compromising DPod1, Coronin, Cortactin, or Scar led to faster recovery times, although to varying degrees.
source: Finally, we measured cap recovery rates when the individual ANRPs were disrupted. Similar to disrupting Arp2/3 or Dia function, compromising DPod1, Coronin, Cortactin, or Scar led to faster recovery times, although to varying degrees (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B,E).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing FRAP data.

claim: DPod1 disruption was almost comparable to disrupting Arp2/3 function in its effect on recovery times and immobile fractions.
source: Interestingly, DPod1 disruption was almost comparable to disrupting Arp2/3 function in its effect on recovery times and immobile fractions.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing experimental findings.

claim: Actin intensities in the various disrupted backgrounds appear to well-reflect the degree to which specific actin networks are the predominant G-actin utilizing networks in the embryo.
source: By analogy to the above, this could also suggest that actin intensities in the various disrupted backgrounds appear to well-reflect the degree to which specific actin networks are the predominant G-actin utilizing networks in the embryo.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The mito-tagged ANRPs are each capable of recruiting Arp3:GFP.

claim: An ANRP-less mito-tag control did not recruit Arp3:GFP.
source: Intriguingly, the mito-tagged ANRPs are each capable of recruiting Arp3:GFP, although an ANRP-less mito-tag control did not (Figure 6A–J, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by figure references showing experimental data.

claim: Mito-tagged ANRPs appear able to activate Arp2/3 complex function, as filamentous actin is observed at the mito-tag puncta.

claim: Of the tested ANRPs, mito-DPod1 possessed the strongest colocalization and recruitment ability.

claim: Scar has moderate Arp3 colocalization but high recruitment ability.

claim: Arp3 recruitment was very high in the double mito-DPod1+mito-Scar background.

claim: DPod1 and Scar are potent activators of Arp2/3 recruitment and activity.
source: This is again consistent with a potential inhibitory interaction between Coronin and Cortactin and with DPod1 and Scar being potent activators of Arp2/3 recruitment and activity.
